summary.en: The Buddha's teaching spread from the Ganges valley under Emperor Ashoka's patronage, then along the Silk Road and maritime trade routes across Central, East and Southeast Asia.

note.en: Enlightenment of Siddhartha Gautama (exact date disputed)
The Buddha's first sermon in the Deer Park
Ashoka patronises Buddhism and sends out missions
Mission of Mahinda, Ashoka's son
By tradition, the White Horse Temple is founded
Baekje king sends a Buddha statue and sutras (538 or 552)
King Songtsen Gampo and his queens build the first temples
Chinese pilgrim Yijing finds a thousand monks here
Altan Khan meets Sonam Gyatso and names him Dalai Lama
Russian authorities recognise Buddhism among the Buryats

summary.en: From Jerusalem Christianity spread through Roman cities, became the empire's faith, then reached Europe via missions and royal baptisms, and the Americas and Asia with colonisation.

note.en: Preaching and crucifixion of Jesus; the first apostolic community
Disciples are first called Christians here
Armenia becomes the first Christian state
Constantine dedicates a new Christian capital
Frumentius converts King Ezana
Baptism of Clovis
Mission of Alopen, recorded on the Xi'an Stele
Baptism of Khan Boris
Baptism of Rus' under Prince Vladimir
Christianisation of Lithuania after the Union of Krewo
First Mass in the New World

summary.en: Islam arose in the Hijaz and within a century of Arab conquest stretched from Spain to the Indus; traders, Sufis and new dynasties then carried it to the Volga, West Africa, India and Indonesia.

note.en: Muhammad begins his prophetic mission
The Hijra; start of the Islamic calendar
Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses into Spain
Campaign of Muhammad ibn Qasim
The Abbasids found a new capital
The caliph's embassy with Ibn Fadlan
Trans-Saharan trade brings Islam to the Sahel
Ghurid conquest, later the Delhi Sultanate
Tombstone of Sultan Malik al-Salih
Khan Özbeg makes Islam the state religion

summary.en: Papermaking stayed Chinese for centuries, reached the Arabs via Samarkand, then entered Europe through Islamic Spain and Italy, where paper mills prepared the ground for printing.

note.en: Cai Lun improves papermaking
Legend credits Chinese prisoners taken at Talas
First paper mill under Harun al-Rashid
Earliest known papermaking in Europe
Watermarks and gelatin-sized paper
Ulman Stromer's mill, the first in Germany
First paper mill on the Ucha river
First paper mill in the Americas

summary.en: Gutenberg's movable-type press spread from Mainz across Europe with German printers, then to the Americas and Asia with missionaries and colonial authorities.

note.en: Gutenberg prints; his Bible is finished c. 1455
Sweynheym and Pannartz open Italy's first press
John of Speyer; Venice soon leads European printing
Caxton, trained in Cologne, sets up his press
Hebrew press of Jewish exiles from Spain
Juan Pablos opens the first press in the Americas
Jesuits open the first press in Asia
Ivan Fyodorov prints the Apostol
First press in British North America

summary.en: Plague reached Kaffa with the Golden Horde's army; Genoese ships carried it to Mediterranean ports, and within five years it swept Europe, killing perhaps up to half the population.

note.en: Plague strikes Khan Jani Beg's army besieging Kaffa
Genoese galleys bring plague to Europe
One of the world's largest cities loses up to a third
Ship isolation introduced, a precursor of quarantine
Boccaccio describes it in the Decameron
A ship from Gascony brings plague to England
An English ship carries plague to Norway
The first Rus' city struck by the pestilence
Grand Prince Simeon and Metropolitan Theognostus die

summary.en: Domesticated in the Andes, the potato reached Europe on Spanish ships, long remained a curiosity, then in the 1700s its yields made it the staple of the poor from Ireland to Russia.

note.en: Spaniards first encounter the potato in the Andes, where it was domesticated millennia earlier
Earliest record outside the Americas
A hospital buys potatoes for its patients
Botanist Clusius receives tubers and describes them
Frederick II's 'Potato Order'
The Senate orders the growing of 'earth apples'
Parmentier, who ate potatoes as a Prussian POW, promotes them

summary.en: Steam railways were born in England's coalfields; within fifty years British locomotives and engineers had carried them to every continent, cutting journeys from weeks to days.

note.en: First public steam-hauled railway
First intercity passenger line
First steam passenger line on the Continent
Russia's first railway, from St Petersburg
The St Petersburg–Moscow line opens
India's first passenger train
First US transcontinental railroad completed
Japan's first line, built by British engineers
Trans-Siberian begun; all-Russian through route by 1916

summary.en: Discovered by Chinese alchemists and weaponised under the Song, gunpowder passed via the Mongols and the Islamic world to Europe, then returned to Asia with Ottoman and Portuguese guns.

note.en: Taoist texts warn of a flammable saltpetre mixture
Wujing Zongyao records the first gunpowder formulas
Mongol invaders use explosive bombs
Hasan al-Rammah describes gunpowder recipes
A document orders cannon and balls
The English field cannon in battle
Guns on the walls against Tokhtamysh
Babur, with Ottoman gunners, defeats Lodi

summary.en: Huge rough stones set upright, in circles or as houses for the dead
Coiled and twisted beasts in gold and felt — the art of the Great Steppe's nomads
Greek form after Alexander: passion, motion and theatrical scale from the Nile to the Indus
Concrete, arch and dome serving the empire; truthful portraits and chronicle reliefs
The Buddha in a Greek mantle: Hellenistic sculpture in the service of Buddhism
Gold mosaics and a heaven-like dome: the church as paradise, the icon as a window to eternity
Inscriptions, ornament and arches instead of images: a space of prayer with no depiction of God
Sandstone temple-mountain: a model of the cosmos with five towers and miles of reliefs
Cross-in-square churches of thin brick or white stone: Byzantine plan, Rus silhouette
Thick walls, round arches and stone vaults: a fortress-church for pilgrims
Pointed vaults, flying buttresses and stained glass: the wall dissolves into coloured light
Horseshoe arches, carved stucco and water in courtyards: al-Andalus's paradise in stone
The book painting as a garden: jewel-bright pigments, high horizon, no shadows
Antiquity measured anew: linear perspective, anatomy and proportion as the measure of man
Renaissance harmony deliberately unbalanced: stretched bodies, cold colour, crowded space
An answer to Hagia Sophia: a central dome on cascading half-domes and pencil-thin minarets
Thin white porcelain painted in cobalt and enamels: the first global brand, carried across the seas
Art designed to overwhelm: motion, dramatic light and theatre that pulls the viewer in
Baroque moved from the state hall to the boudoir: asymmetric shell-work, pastels and playful love
A return to Greece and Rome after the excavations: strict orders, clear contour, civic virtue
Feeling and the elements over reason: the lone hero, storm, ruins and the national past

A fleeting moment of light and air, caught outdoors in separate strokes of pure colour

Objects broken into facets and shown from several viewpoints at once on the flat canvas

Machine-age luxury: geometry, gleaming metal and the stepped silhouette
